title: GPU storm predictive priming and tenant soft-throttle playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description: After the hosted-API capacity incident on 2025-01-12 where simultaneous tenant bursts caused multi-pool GPU exhaustion and queue amplification, we need an operational playbook plus two engineering deliverables: (1) a predictive priming probe that pre-warms pools for forecasted bursts, and (2) a tenant soft-throttle mechanism that gracefully limits admission with per-tenant grace windows and backoff. This ticket coordinates the investigation, design, implementation, tests, and rollout.

investigation: Root-cause summary: concurrent high-concurrency workloads from ~8 tenants triggered a correlated burst pattern. Autoscaler reacted late due to aggregation hysteresis and cold-start kernel scheduling overheads (model variants with long first-token kernels). Admission control admitted inflight requests without tenant-level caps; queue amplification occurred when a small fraction of long-sequence requests blocked GPU slots while short requests queued. Telemetry gaps: request-level KV cache hit metrics and tenant-prefetch signals were missing, making it hard to predict kernel priming needs.
findings:
1) Autoscaler hysteresis + conservative scale thresholds caused >3 minute lag to reach needed capacity during correlated bursts.
2) Kernel priming cost (first-compile/first-token latency) can magnify capacity needs for certain model variants.
3) Lack of tenant-scoped admission caps allowed noisy neighbor amplification.
4) Prefix/KV cache warming behaviour not exposed in metrics.
5) Existing fallback to smaller model variants was not automated for multi-tenant contention scenarios.
decisions:
1) Implement a predictive priming probe: short probe threads estimate imminent priming cost based on recent request traces and warm the kernel path on candidate nodes before scale-up.
2) Add tenant soft-throttle: configurable grace window (default 90s) with progressive backoff and priority weight to reduce sudden admission from the same tenant.
3) Expose KV cache hit-rate, kernel-primed boolean, and per-tenant queued-count as first-class telemetry to Console.
4) Keep manual emergency eviction playbook but automate preemptive eviction in purely host-owned low-priority lanes.
5) Rollout changes to staging -> canary (10% traffic) -> global after 2 days of canary stability and automated rollback on increased 5xxs.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Predictive priming probe runs in staging and reduces observed first-token kernel cost for targeted model variants by >20% during synthetic bursts.
2) Tenant soft-throttle enforces a per-tenant grace period and backoff without increasing 5xxs in canary traffic.
3) New telemetry surfaces (KV hit-rate, kernel-primed, per-tenant queued-count) appear in Console with alerts.
4) Integration tests (tenant-sim) show <10% increase in mean latency across tenants and >25% reduction in peak queue length for tested bursts.
test_plan: Unit tests for admission score calculation. Integration tests: tenant-sim harness with controlled burst patterns (short-heavy, long-heavy, mixed). Canary test: enable on 10% traffic for 48 hours, monitor 5xxs, tail latency, queue sizes, and autoscaler decisions. Automated rollback if 5xx rate increases by >50% relative to baseline.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge behind feature flag. 2) Deploy to staging; run tenant-sim and validate metrics. 3) Canary on a small subset of hosts (10%). 4) Expand to 50% if stable for 48h. 5) Global rollout and remove flag after 7 days of stable operation. Post-rollout retrospective and metrics collection window = 14 days.
notes: Keep an eye on kernel-priming CPU cost on priming nodes; priming too many nodes will increase idle cost. Tradeoff: slightly higher prewarm cost vs reduced tail latency and fewer emergency scale events. Consider future work: automated fallback to quantized variants during pool pressure and tenant-weighted admission fairness algorithm improvements.
